claim: More than 50% of proteins/enzymes identified in sequenced eubacterial and archaeal genomes have uncertain or unknown in vitro activities and in vivo physiological functions.
source: >50% of the proteins/enzymes so identified have uncertain or unknown in vitro activities and in vivo physiological functions.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of genome annotation presented in the introduction without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: Metabolic pathways in eubacteria and archaea are often encoded by operons and/or gene clusters (genome neighborhoods).
source: Metabolic pathways in eubacteria and archaea often are encoded by operons and/or gene clusters (genome neighborhoods) that provide important clues for assignment of both enzyme functions and metabolic pathways.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction.

claim: The genome neighborhood network (GNN) approach enables large scale prediction of in vitro enzymatic activities and in vivo physiological functions of uncharacterized enzymes in protein families.
source: We describe a bioinformatic approach (genome neighborhood network; GNN) that enables large scale prediction of the in vitro enzymatic activities and in vivo physiological functions (metabolic pathways) of uncharacterized enzymes in protein families.
evidence: This is the main methodological claim of the paper, supported by the experimental validation described throughout.

claim: In vitro activities were measured for 51 proteins in 12 families in the proline racemase superfamily representing approximately 85% of the sequences.
source: The predictions were verified by measuring in vitro activities for 51 proteins in 12 families in the PRS that represent ~85% of the sequences
evidence: This is a summary of experimental work presented in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Three enzymatic activities have been previously described for the proline racemase superfamily: proline racemase (ProR), 4R-hydroxyproline 2-epimerase (4HypE), and trans 3-hydroxy-L-proline dehydratase (t3HypD).
source: Three enzymatic activities have been described for the PRS: proline racemase (ProR; eubacteria [Stadtman et al., 1957] and eukaryotes [Reina-San-Martín et al., 2000], 4R-hydroxyproline 2-epimerase (4HypE; eubacteria [Adams and Frank, 1980; Goytia et al., 2007; Gavina et al., 2010]), and trans 3-hydroxy-L-proline dehydratase (t3HypD; eukaryotes [Visser et al., 2012] and eubacteria [Watanabe et al., 2014])
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previously characterized ProRs and 4HypEs catalyze racemization/epimerization of the α-carbon using two general acidic/basic Cys residues located on opposite faces of the active site.
source: The previously characterized ProRs and 4HypEs catalyze racemization/epimerization of the a-carbon in a 1,1-proton transfer mechanism that, in the structurally characterized enzymes, uses two general acidic/basic Cys residues located on opposite faces of the active site (Buschiazzo et al., 2006; Rubinstein and Major, 2009).
evidence: This mechanistic information is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The syn-dehydration reaction catalyzed by t3HypD requires a general basic catalyst to abstract the proton from the α-carbon.
source: The syn-dehydration reaction catalyzed by t3HypD requires a general basic catalyst to abstract the proton from the a-carbon; its conjugate acid likely functions as the general acidic catalyst to facilitate departure of the 3-hydroxyl group.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the chemical nature of the reaction.

claim: Sequence alignment of functionally characterized t3HypDs and ProRs suggests the presence of a single active site Cys residue in t3HypDs, with the second Cys in ProR replaced by a Thr residue.
source: Sequence alignment of the functionally characterized t3HypDs and ProRs suggests the presence of a single active site Cys residue in the active sites of the t3HypDs (the second Cys in ProR is replaced by a Thr residue).
evidence: This is based on computational sequence alignment analysis.

claim: The proline racemase superfamily SSN contains 2333 unique sequences from InterPro family IPR008794.
source: A sequence similarity network (SSN) (Atkinson et al., 2009) for 2333 unique sequences in the PRS (InterPro family IPR008794; release 43.0) was constructed
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data used in the analysis.

claim: At an e-value threshold of 10^-55 (>~35% sequence identity), the majority of PRS members are located in a single functionally heterogeneous cluster.
source: When the network is displayed with an e-value threshold of 10-55 (> ~35% sequence identity is required to draw an edge [line] between nodes [proteins]), the majority of the members of the PRS are located in a single functionally heterogeneous cluster (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the SSN visualization shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At an e-value threshold of 10^-110 (~60% sequence identity), the PRS separates into 28 clusters and 49 singletons.
source: As the e-value threshold stringency is increased to 10-110 (sequence identity required to draw an edge is increased to > ~60%), the PRS separates into 28 clusters and 49 singletons (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the SSN visualization shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Previously characterized ProR, 4HypE, and t3HypD functions are located in separate clusters at the 10^-110 e-value threshold.
source: At the e-value threshold of 10-110 (Figure 2B) the nodes for the experimentally characterized functions—ProR (magenta; cluster 7), 4HypE (blue and red; clusters 1 and 2, respectively), and t3HypD (brown; cluster 8)—are located in separate clusters that account for ~30% of the sequences in the PRS.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 2B and represents the separation of known functions.

claim: Separated clusters at the 10^-110 e-value threshold are expected to be isofunctional because their active sites are formed from conserved amino acid residues.
source: At the e-value threshold of 10-110 (Figure 2B), the separated clusters are expected to be isofunctional because, from sequence alignments, their active sites are formed from conserved amino acid residues (acid/base catalysts and specificity determining residues).
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation patterns.

claim: The GNN for the PRS was constructed by collecting genome neighbors (±10 genes) for all PRS members and performing an all-by-all BLAST displayed at an e-value threshold of 10^-20.
source: After collecting the genome neighbors, we assign each of them the same color as the color of the query; with this strategy, proteins that are encoded by the same genome neighborhood as the query are easily identified in the GNN because they share the same color as the query. We then perform an all-by-all BLAST on the sequences of the genome neighbors and display the results as an SSN using an e-value threshold of 10-20
evidence: This describes the computational methodology used to construct the GNN.

claim: At the 10^-20 e-value threshold, most clusters in the GNN contain members of distinct protein families and superfamilies.
source: Using this e-value threshold, most of the clusters in the GNN contain the members of distinct protein families and superfamilies (e.g., Pfam families)
evidence: This is an observation about the clustering behavior at the chosen threshold.

claim: ProR function is encoded by anaerobic eubacteria that ferment L-proline and is represented by the magenta cluster (cluster 7) in the SSN.
source: As a retrospective use of the GNN, the ProR function is encoded by anaerobic eubacteria that ferment L-proline and is represented by the magenta cluster (cluster 7) in the SSN (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as known information used to validate the GNN approach.

claim: The first step in the catabolism of L-proline is racemization to D-proline by ProR, which is then reduced to 2-keto-5-aminopentanoate by D-proline reductase (PrdAB).
source: The first step in the catabolism of L-proline is racemization to D-proline (by ProR) that is reduced to 2-keto-5-aminopentanoate by D-proline reductase (Kabisch et al., 1999) (by PrdAB; Figure 1).
evidence: This pathway information is supported by a citation and shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the GNN, the clusters for PrdA and PrdB polypeptides in D-proline reductase are uniformly magenta, consistent with colocalization with ProR genes.
source: In the GNN, the clusters for the PrdA and PrdB polypeptides in D-proline reductase are uniformly magenta, as expected if the genes encoding ProR and PrdAB are colocalized with the gene encoding ProR (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is observed in the GNN visualization in Figure 3B,C and validates the approach.

claim: The lack of other colors in the PrdAB clusters in the GNN implies that no other clusters in the SSN have the ProR function.
source: The lack of other colors in the PrdAB clusters in the GNN implies that no other clusters in the SSN have the ProR function.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the color patterns in the GNN.

claim: The 4HypE function has been assigned to members of the blue (cluster 1) and red (cluster 2) clusters in the SSN.
source: As a second retrospective example, the 4HypE function has been assigned to members of the blue (cluster 1) and red (cluster 2) clusters in the SSN (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as previously known information used for validation.

claim: In the GNN, clusters identified by the blue and red clusters include the D-amino acid oxidase (DAAO), dihydrodipicolinate synthase (DHDPS), and aldehyde dehydrogenase superfamilies.
source: In the GNN, clusters identified by the blue and red clusters include the D-amino acid oxidase (DAAO; Figure 3D) (Watanabe et al., 2012), dihydrodipicolinate synthase (DHDPS; Figure 3E) (Singh and Adams, 1965; Watanabe et al., 2012), and aldehyde dehydrogenase (Figure 3F) (Koo and Adams, 1974; Watanabe et al., 2007) superfamilies
evidence: This is observed in the GNN and supported by citations to previous work on these pathways.

claim: The catabolic pathway for trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline can be initiated by epimerization of t4Hyp to cis-4-hydroxy-D-proline by 4HypE, followed by reactions catalyzed by c4Hyp oxidase, c4Hyp imino acid dehydratase/deaminase, and α-ketoglutarate semialdehyde dehydrogenase.
source: As we and others recently established for organisms that use trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline betaine as sole carbon and nitrogen source (Zhao et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2014), the catabolic pathway for trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline (t4Hyp) (Figure 1) can be initiated by the epimerization of t4Hyp to cis-4-hydroxy-D-proline (c4Hyp) by 4HypE, followed by reactions catalyzed by c4Hyp oxidase (a member of the DAAO superfamily), c4Hyp imino acid dehydratase/deaminase (a member of the DHDPS superfamily), and a-ketoglutarate semialdehyde dehydrogenase (a member of the aldehyde dehydrogenase superfamily).
evidence: This pathway is supported by recent publications and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The DAAO, DHDPS, and aldehyde dehydrogenase clusters in the GNN also contain nodes with orange (cluster 9), pale green (cluster 11), and teal (cluster 4) colors from the SSN.
source: The DAAO (Figure 3D), DHDPS (Figure 3E), and aldehyde dehydrogenase (Figure 3F) clusters also contain nodes with other colors from the SSN (Figure 2B), including orange (cluster 9), pale green (cluster 11), and teal (cluster 4).
evidence: This is observed in the GNN visualizations in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Members of the orange and pale green clusters catalyze the 4HypE reaction.
source: Proteins from the orange and pale green clusters were purified and assayed using a library of proline derivatives (Figure 4). As expected, members of the orange and pale green clusters catalyze the 4HypE reaction (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by experimental enzyme assays shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Bacillus cereus ATCC14579 (cluster 4, teal) and Streptomyces lividans TK24 (cluster 11, pale green) both utilize t4Hyp as sole carbon source.
source: As predicted from the GNN, Bacillus cereus ATCC14579 (cluster 4, teal) and Streptomyces lividans TK24 (cluster 11, pale green) both utilize t4Hyp as sole carbon source (Table 3)
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth phenotype experiments shown in Table 3.

claim: The genes encoding the predicted 4HypEs and proximal genes encoding the predicted c4Hyp oxidases, c4Hyp imino acid dehydratase/deaminases, and α-ketoglutarate semialdehyde dehydrogenases are up-regulated when the encoding organism is grown on t4Hyp as carbon source.
source: also, the genes encoding the predicted 4HypEs (Table 4) and the proximal genes encoding the predicted c4Hyp oxidases, c4Hyp imino acid dehydratase/deaminases, and a-ketoglutarate semialdehyde dehydrogenases (Table 5) are up-regulated when the encoding organism is grown on t4Hyp as carbon source (Table 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by transcriptomic data shown in Tables 4 and 5.

claim: Purified proteins from the orange groups are promiscuous for the 3HypE reaction, but their genome neighborhood context identifies their physiological functions as 4HypE.
source: The purified proteins from the orange groups are promiscuous for the 3HypE reaction (Tables 1 and 2), but their genome neighborhood context identifies their physiological functions as 4HypE.
evidence: This is based on both enzyme assay data (Tables 1 and 2) and genome context analysis.

claim: The X-ray structure of Q4KGU2 (locus tag: PFL_1412; red, cluster 2) was determined in the presence of t4Hyp and pyrrole-2-carboxylate (PYC).
source: The X-ray structure of one of the previously functionally assigned 4HypEs (Uniprot: Q4KGU2; locus tag: PFL_1412; red, cluster 2) was determined in the presence of the substrate, t4Hyp and, also, pyrrole-2-carboxylate (PYC), a stable analogue of the enolate anion intermediate (Figure 5A,B; Table 6).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by crystallographic data in Table 6 and structures shown in Figure 5.

claim: The structures of Q4KGU2 with t4Hyp and PYC are the first liganded structures of a 4HypE and the first structure of a PRS with an authentic substrate.
source: These are the first liganded structures of a 4HypE and the first structure of a PRS with an authentic substrate.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the structural data.

claim: The structures of Q4KGU2 corroborate the positioning of the active site Cys/Cys pair (Cys 88, Cys 236) to facilitate substrate epimerization.
source: These structures corroborate the positioning of the active site Cys/Cys pair (Cys 88, Cys 236) to facilitate substrate epimerization, highlight residues specific to the coordination of the 4-hydroxyl group, and validate the hypothesis that PYC and substrate bind in a similar fashion.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structures shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: The X-ray structure of B9K4G4 (locus tag: Avi_7022; orange, cluster 8) was determined in the presence of t4Hyp.
source: In addition, the X-ray structure of one of the newly functionally assigned 4HypEs (Uniprot: B9K4G4; locus tag: Avi_7022; orange, cluster 8) was determined in the presence of its substrate, t4Hyp.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by crystallographic data in Table 6.

claim: The active site of B9K4G4 contains Ser 93 on one face and Cys 255 on the opposite face.
source: The active site contains Ser 93 on one face and Cys 255 on the opposite face (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Despite the conserved ability of B9K4G4 to catalyze the 4HypE reaction, the Cys-Cys general acid/base pair observed in Q4KGU2 is not conserved.
source: Thus, despite the conserved ability of this enzyme to catalyze the 4HypE reaction (a two-base 1,1-proton transfer reaction), the Cys–Cys general acid/base pair observed in the structure of Q4KGU2 from the red cluster is not conserved.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the two crystal structures and enzyme activity data.

claim: The structural diversity in the PRS highlights convergent evolution of the 4HypE function.
source: This observation highlights the structural diversity associated with evolution of function in the PRS. Without the information provided by the GNNs, the 4HypE function would not have been expected.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and functional data showing different catalytic residues performing the same reaction.

claim: Members of the navy cluster (cluster 5; species of Bacilli) identify several clusters in the GNN, including families of TRAP and ABC transport systems, peptidases, and a family in the ornithine cyclodeaminase superfamily (OCDS).
source: However, the members of the navy cluster (cluster 5; species of Bacilli) identify several clusters in the GNN, including families of the components of TRAP and ABC transport systems, families of peptidases, and a family in the ornithine cyclodeaminase superfamily (OCDS)
evidence: This is observed in the GNN analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Members of the OCDS catalyze NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H-dependent reactions that involve the ketimines obtained by oxidation of α-amino acids.
source: Members of the OCDS catalyze NAD(P)+/NAD(P)H-dependent reactions that involve the ketimines obtained by oxidation of a-amino acids (Goodman et al., 2004; Schröder et al., 2004; Gatto et al., 2006)
evidence: This is stated as known information supported by citations.

claim: Some members of the OCDS have been reported to catalyze the reduction of the ketimine of proline and oxidation of L-proline.
source: some have been reported to catalyze the reduction of the ketimine of proline (Hallen et al., 2011) (and oxidation of L-proline; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Members of both the navy (cluster 5) and olive (cluster 12) clusters in the SSN catalyze the t3HypD reaction.
source: Using purified proteins, we determined that members of both the navy (cluster 5) and olive (cluster 12) clusters in the SSN catalyze the t3HypD reaction (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental enzyme assays shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Members of the OCDS cluster catalyze the NADPH-dependent reduction of the ketimine of proline to form L-proline.
source: We also determined that members of the OCDS cluster catalyze the NADPH-dependent reduction of the ketimine of proline to form L-proline (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental enzyme assays shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The catabolic pathway for trans-3-hydroxy-L-proline proceeds by dehydration, nonenzymatic tautomerization of the dehydration product to the ketimine of proline, and reduction of the ketimine to form L-proline.
source: The catabolic pathway for trans-3-hydroxy-L-proline is known to proceed by dehydration, nonenzymatic tautomerization of the dehydration product to the ketimine of proline and, finally, reduction of the ketimine to form L-proline (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as known information and shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the OCDS SSN, the previously characterized proline ketimine reductases are located in clusters/families distinct from the members of the OCDS identified in the GNN.
source: In the OCDS SSN (Figure 6A), the previously characterized proline ketimine reductases are located in clusters/families distinct from the members of the OCDS identified in our GNN.
evidence: This is observed in the OCDS SSN shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Assignment of the t3HypD function to the members of navy and olive clusters in the SSN would not have been possible without the synergistic information contained in the GNN.
source: Thus, assignment of the t3HypD function to the members of navy and olive clusters in the SSN would not have been possible without the synergistic information contained in the GNN.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis showing that GNN provided essential information for functional assignment.

claim: The structure of t3HypD B9K4G4 from the light sky blue cluster (cluster 3) was determined in the presence of PYC.
source: We determined the structure of a t3HypD (B9K4G4) from the light sky blue cluster (cluster 3) in the presence of PYC (Table 6).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by crystallographic data in Table 6.

claim: B9K4G4 contains Ser 90 in a similar conformation as B9JQV3 from the orange cluster and Thr 256 on the opposing face, instead of the typical PRS Cys/Cys pair.
source: Instead of the typical PRS Cys/Cys pair, B9K4G4 contains Ser 90 in a similar conformation as was determined for B9JQV3 from the orange cluster (4HypE activity) and Thr 256 on the opposing face (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The assignment of function enabled by the GNNs identifies convergent evolution of function within the PRS.
source: Again, the assignment of function enabled by the GNNs identifies convergent evolution of function within the PRS.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation of different catalytic residues performing similar functions.

claim: Members of the light sky blue (cluster 3) cluster in the SSN identify the same superfamilies as both the 4HypE and t3HypD clusters, including transport systems, transcriptional regulators, DAAO, DHDPS, aldehyde dehydrogenase, and OCD.
source: Members of the light sky blue (cluster 3) cluster in the SSN identify the same (super)families identified by both the 4HypE and t3HypD clusters (transport systems, transcriptional regulators, DAAO [Figure 3D], DHDPS [Figure 3E], aldehyde dehydrogenase [Figure 3F], and OCD [Figure 3G])
evidence: This is observed in the GNN analysis shown in Figures 3D-G.

claim: Several members of the light sky blue cluster identify a GNN cluster annotated as the malate/L-lactate dehydrogenase 2 superfamily (MLD2).
source: however, several members of the light sky blue cluster identify a GNN cluster annotated as the malate/L-lactate dehydrogenase 2 superfamily (MLD2; NADH-dependent oxidoreductases) (Muramatsu et al., 2005) (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is observed in the GNN shown in Figure 3H and supported by a citation.

claim: The light sky blue cluster is functionally heterogeneous and some members are promiscuous for the 4HypE and t3HypD functions.
source: Using purified members of the PRS, we determined that the light sky blue cluster is functionally heterogeneous (and some members are promiscuous) for the 4HypE and t3HypD functions (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental enzyme assays shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Members of the MLD2 superfamily in the GNN catalyze the reduction of proline ketimine.
source: We also determined that members of the MLD2 superfamily in the GNN catalyze the reduction of proline ketimine (Table 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental enzyme assays shown in Table 7.

claim: The GNN provided essential information for predicting/assigning functions to the members of the light sky blue cluster in the PRS SSN.
source: Thus, the GNN provided essential information for predicting/assigning functions to the members of the light sky blue cluster in the PRS SSN.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined analysis of GNN and experimental validation.

claim: In several species, two members of the PRS are encoded by proximal genes (a 4HypE and a t3HypD), and these species can utilize both t4Hyp and trans-3-hydroxy-L-proline as carbon and nitrogen sources.
source: For example, in several species, two members of the PRS are encoded by proximal genes, that is, a 4HypE and a t3HypD; these species can utilize both t4Hyp and trans-3-hydroxy-L-proline as carbon and nitrogen sources.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the genome context analysis.

claim: The GNN contains a cluster for the PRS where each PRS finds the adjacent PRS when used as query.
source: Thus, the GNN contains a cluster for the PRS (right-hand cluster in the top row [when used as query, each PRS finds the adjacent PRS; Figure 3I]).
evidence: This is observed in the GNN shown in Figure 3I.

claim: For species with proximal 4HypE and t3HypD genes, clusters in the GNN are a composite of two genome contexts representing proteins/enzymes that participate in both catabolic pathways.
source: For these species, clusters in the GNN are a composite of two genome contexts, that is, the proteins/enzymes that participate in both catabolic pathways.
evidence: This is an inference about how the GNN represents complex genome contexts.

claim: Several purified proteins catalyze both the 4HypE and t3HypD reactions.
source: Several of the purified proteins catalyze both the 4HypE and t3HypD reactions (Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental enzyme assays shown in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Some promiscuous proteins identify both the OCD or MLD2 superfamilies (predicting the t3HypD pathway) and the DAAO, DHDPS, and aldehyde dehydrogenase superfamilies (predicting the 4HypE pathway) in their genome neighborhoods.
source: Some of these promiscuous proteins identify both the OCD or MLD2 superfamilies (predicting the t3HypD pathway) and the DAAO, DHDPS, and aldehyde dehydrogenase superfamilies (predicting the 4HypE pathway) in their genome neighborhoods (Figure 7).
evidence: This is observed in the GNN analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The in vitro promiscuity of some proteins is not an artifact but is physiologically significant based on genome neighborhood context.
source: In these cases, we conclude that the in vitro promiscuity is not an 'artifact' but is physiologically significant.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation between in vitro activity and genome context.

claim: The majority of the members of the PRS catalyze only the three previously characterized reactions (ProR, 4HypE, and t3HypD).
source: As established in this study, the majority of the members of the PRS catalyze only the three previously characterized (known) reactions (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental characterization of 51 proteins.

claim: The GNN was used to correctly predict functions for all of the highly populated clusters/families representing more than 85% of the PRS members.
source: As a result, we were able to use the GNN without any additional information to correctly predict functions for all of the highly populated clusters/families (>85% of the members; Figure 8).
evidence: This is a summary of the predictive success of the GNN approach shown in Figure 8.

claim: The use of GNNs is restricted to enzymes that are encoded by proximal operons and/or gene clusters in eubacteria and archaea.
source: The use of GNNs is restricted to those enzymes that are encoded by proximal operons and/or gene clusters in eubacteria and archaea.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the GNN approach.

claim: For Escherichia coli K-12, 60% of the genes are located in polycistronic transcriptional units that may provide linked functional information.
source: For Escherichia coli K-12, 60% of the genes are located in polycistronic transcriptional units that may provide linked functional information that can be used to identify pathways; 40% are located in monocistronic transcriptional units (http://regulondb.ccg.unam.mx/menu/tools/regulondb_overviews/chart_form.jsp).
evidence: This is stated as known information with a reference to a database.

claim: Genome neighborhood context is not a general solution to infer functions for many proteins/enzymes of unknown function encoded in eubacterial and archaeal genomes.
source: Thus, genome neighborhood context is not a general solution to infer functions for many proteins/enzymes of unknown function encoded eubacterial and archaeal genomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the limitations of the GNN approach.

claim: Complete metabolic pathways may be encoded by multiple transcriptional units that are not genome proximal and may be recognized by regulon analyses.
source: Even for those proteins encoded by polycistronic transcriptional units, complete metabolic pathways may be encoded by multiple transcriptional units (mono- and/or polycistronic) that are not genome proximal; these pathways and their component enzymes and ligand binding proteins (solute binding proteins for transport systems and transcriptional regulators) may be recognized by regulon analyses that identify conserved binding sites for transcriptional regulators (Ravcheev et al., 2013; Rodionov et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a complementary approach with supporting citations.

claim: Genome neighborhoods and/or regulons allow the identification of components of unknown/novel metabolic pathways, and the locations of these proteins/enzymes in SSNs provide restrictions on their ligand/substrate specificities and/or reaction mechanisms.
source: To the extent that genome neighborhoods and/or regulons allow the identification of the components of unknown/novel metabolic pathways, the locations of these proteins/enzymes in the SSNs for their (super)families will provide restrictions on their ligand/substrate specificities and/or reaction mechanisms (Atkinson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a general principle stated with a supporting citation.

claim: In silico (virtual) docking of ligand libraries to multiple binding proteins and enzymes in an unknown metabolic pathway (pathway docking) is a powerful approach to enhance the reliability of docking to predict novel ligand/substrate specificities and identify novel metabolic pathways.
source: Also, as we recently demonstrated (Zhao et al., 2013), in silico (virtual) docking of ligand libraries to multiple binding proteins and enzymes in an unknown metabolic pathway (pathway docking) is a powerful approach to enhance the reliability of docking to predict novel ligand/substrate specificities and identify novel metabolic pathways
evidence: This is stated as a complementary approach with a supporting citation.

claim: GNNs provide a novel approach for large-scale analysis and visualization of genome neighborhood context in enzyme superfamilies.
source: Irrespective of the many complications associated with assignment of function to unknown proteins/enzymes, we conclude that GNNs provide a novel approach for large-scale analysis and visualization of genome neighborhood context in enzyme (super)families.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper based on the demonstrated utility of the approach.

claim: The SSNs for the PRS and OCDS were created using Pythoscape v1.0.
source: The SSNs for the PRS (Figure 2) and the OCDS (Figure 5A) were created using Pythoscape v1.0 (Barber and Babbit, 2012) that is available for download from http://www.rbvi.ucsf.edu/trac/Pythoscape
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the computational tools used.

claim: The input sequences for the SSNs were downloaded from the InterPro webpages of PRS and OCDS.
source: The input sequences were downloaded from the InterPro webpages of PRS and OCDS: http://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro/entry/IPR008794, http://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro/entry/IPR003462, respectively.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the data sources.

claim: Cytoscape v2.8 is used for visualization and analysis of the SSN.
source: Cytoscape v2.8 (Smoot et al., 2011) is used for visualization and analysis of the SSN.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the visualization tools used.

claim: The GNN for the PRS was created using Pythoscape v1.0.
source: The GNN for the PRS (Figure 3) was also created using Pythoscape v1.0 (Barber and Babbit, 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the computational tools used.

claim: At an e-value cutoff 10^-110, each cluster in the SSN was assigned a unique cluster number and color for labeling genome context sequences.
source: At an e-value cutoff 10-110, each cluster in the SSN was assigned a unique cluster number and color, which are used for labeling and coloring genome context sequences.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the GNN construction procedure.

claim: Genome context sequences were collected from the ±10 gene range of each PRS member.
source: Genome context sequences were collected from the ±10 gene range of each PRS member and used as the input sequences for making the GNN using the procedure for generating a SSN.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the genome neighborhood collection.

claim: Genes for members of the PRS encoded by genomic DNAs in the Macromolecular Therapeutics Development Facility were cloned into pNIC28-BSA4-based expression vectors.
source: Genes for members of the PRS that are encoded by the genomic DNAs in the Macromolecular Therapeutics Development Facility at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine were cloned into pNIC28-BSA4-based expression vectors as previously described (Sauder et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about protein production with a supporting citation.

claim: The pNIC28-BSA4-based expression plasmids were transformed into Escherichia coli BL21(DE3) containing the pRIL plasmid for protein expression.
